title: Levels of Consciousness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Yogachara model of eight levels of consciousness and sets it beside Lisa Feldman Barrett's Seven and a Half Lessons About the Brain. Nomon describes manas, the seventh level, as a shuttle diplomat carrying reports between the busy thinking mind and the storehouse where seeds of conditioning wait to sprout. Abraham Maslow's pyramid of needs, long a favorite, gets a second look, since the brain keeps tending food and safety all the time. Nomon then reads Barrett's first chapter, which follows the amphioxus, a "stomach on a stick," toward brains that run a body budget by prediction.

Once upon a time, the earth was ruled by creatures without brains.
This is not a political statement, just a biological one.
One of those creatures was the amphioxus.
If you have ever glimpsed one, you will probably mistake it for a little worm until you notice the gill-like slits on either side of the body.
Amphioxus populated the oceans about 550 million years ago, and they lived very simple lives.
An amphioxus could propel itself through the water, thanks to its very basic system for movement, and it had an exceedingly simple way of eating.
It planted itself in the sea floor, like a blade of grass, and consumed any minuscule creatures that happened to drift into its mouth.
Taste and smell were of no concern because an amphioxus did not have senses like yours.
It had no ears, just a few cells to detect changes in light.
It had no eyes, just a few cells that could detect changes in light.
It had no ears, it could not hear.
Its meager, nervous system included a tiny clump of cells that were not really a brain.
An amphioxus, you could say, was like a stomach on a stick.
Amphioxus are your distant cousins, and they are still around today.
When you look at a modern amphioxus, you behold a creature that has been living in the ocean, very similar to your own ancient tiny ancestor who roamed the same seas.
Can you picture a little wormy creature two inches long swaying in the current of a prehistoric ocean and glimpse humanity's evolutionary journey?
It is difficult.
You have so much that the ancient amphioxus did not: a few hundred bones, an abundance of internal organs, some limbs, a nose, a charming smile, and most importantly, a brain.
The amphioxus did not need a brain.
Its cells for sensing were connected to the cells for moving, so it just reacted.
It reacted to its watery world without much processing.

You, however, have an intricate, powerful brain that gives rise to mental events as diverse as thoughts, emotions, memories, and dreams—an internal life that shapes so much of what is distinctive and meaningful about your existence.
Why did a brain like yours evolve?
Well, the obvious answer is to think.

It is common to assume that our brains evolved in some kind of upward progression, say from lower animals to higher animals, with the most sophisticated thinking brain of all, the human brain, at the top.
After all, thinking is the human superpower, right?
Well, the obvious answer turns out to be wrong.
In fact, the idea that our brains evolved for thinking has been a source of many profound misconceptions by human nature.

Once you give up this cherished belief, you will have taken the first step towards understanding how your brain actually works and what its most important job is, and ultimately what kind of creature you really are.
Five hundred million years ago, a little amphioxus and other simple creatures continued to dine serenely on the ocean floor, and the Earth entered what scientists called the Cambrian period.
During this time, something new and significant appeared on the evolutionary scene: hunting.
Somewhere, somehow, one creature was able to sense the presence of another creature and deliberately eat it.
Animals had gobbled one another before, but now the eating was purposeful.
Hunting did not require a brain, but it was a big step towards developing one.
The emergence of predators during the Cambrian period transformed the planet into a more competitive and dangerous place.
Both predators and prey evolved to sense more of the world around them.
They began to develop more sensory systems.
Amphioxus could distinguish light from dark, but newer creatures could actually see.
Amphioxus had simple skin sensation, but newer creatures evolved a fuller sense of their body movements in the water and a greater sense of touch that allowed them to detect objects by vibration.
Sharks today still use this kind of touch sense to locate prey.
With the arrival of greater senses, the most critical question in existence became: is that blob in the distance good to eat, or will it eat me?
Creatures who could better sense their surroundings were more likely to survive and thrive.
Amphioxus may have been a master of its environment, but it could not sense that it even had an environment, and these newer animals could.
The hunters and the hunted also received a boost from another new ability: more sophisticated kinds of movement.
For the amphioxus, whose nerves for sensing and moving were woven together, movement was extremely basic.
Whenever its stream of food became a trickle, it wriggled in a random direction to plant itself in another spot, and any looming shadow prompted its body to dart away.
In the new world of hunting, however, predators and prey alike began to evolve more capable systems for movement, or motor systems, to navigate with greater speed and dexterity.

These newer animals could dart, turn, and dive deliberately towards other things like food, and away from things like threats in ways that suited their environment like no other creature could before.
Once creatures could sense at a distance and make more sophisticated movements, evolution favored those who performed those tasks efficiently.
If they chased a meal but moved too slowly, something else caught the meal and ate it first.
They burned up energy fleeing from a potential threat that never arrived.
They wasted resources that might need later.
Energy efficiency was the key to survival.
You can think about energy efficiency like a budget.
A financial budget tracks money as it is earned and spent, and a budget for your body similarly tracks resources, like water, salt, and glucose, as you gain and lose them.
Each action that spends resources, such as swimming or running, is like a withdrawal from your account.
Actions that replenish your resources, such as eating and sleeping, are like deposits.
This is a simplified explanation, but it captures the key idea that running a body requires biological resources.
Every action you take or do not take is like an economic choice, and your brain is guessing when to spend resources and when to save them.

The best way to keep a financial budget, as you may know from personal experience, is to avoid surprises, to anticipate your financial needs before they arise, and make sure you have the resources to meet them.
The same is true of a body budget.
Little Cambrian creatures needed an energy-efficient way to survive when hungry predators were nearby.
Should they wait around until the ravenous beast made its move and then react by freezing or hiding, or should they anticipate the lunge and prepare their bodies in escaping?
When it came to body budgeting, prediction beats reaction.
I will editorialize a little bit: this is a really important theme she is starting here, prediction.
It is kind of all about prediction.
Prediction beats reaction.
A creature that prepared its movement before the predator struck was more likely to be around tomorrow than a creature that awaited a predator's pounce.
Creatures that predicted correctly most of the time, or made non-fatal mistakes and learned from them, did well.
Those that frequently predicted poorly, or missed threats, or false alarmed about threats that never materialized and used up resources did not do so well.
They explored their environment less, foraged less, and were less likely to reproduce.
The scientific name for body budgeting is allostasis.
It means automatically predicting and preparing to meet the body's needs before they arise.
A Cambrian creature acquired and spent resources throughout the day by sensing and moving.
Allostasis kept the systems of their bodies in balance most of the time.
Withdrawals were fine as long as they renewed the spent resources in a timely manner.
But how can animals predict their body's future needs?
The best source of information comes from their past: the actions they have taken at other times in similar circumstances.
If a past action brought benefits such as a successful escape or a tasty meal, they are likely to repeat that action.
All sorts of animals, including humans, somehow conjure up past experiences to prepare their bodies for action.
Prediction is such a useful capability that even single-celled creatures plan their actions predictably.
Scientists are still puzzling on how they do it.
So imagine a tiny Cambrian creature drifting in the current.
Up ahead, it senses an object that might be tasty to eat.
What now?
It can move, but should it?
After all, moving takes energy from the budget.
The movement should be worth the effort economically speaking.
That is a prediction based on past experience: should we prepare the body for action or not?
To be clear, I do not mean a conscious, thoughtful decision like weighing the pros and cons.
I am saying that something must occur inside a creature to predict and launch one set of movements rather than another.
That something reflects a determination of worth.
The value of a movement is intimately bound up with body budgeting by allostasis.
Meanwhile, ancient animals continued to evolve larger, more complex bodies.
That means the insides of bodies became more sophisticated.
The amphioxus, with that little stomach on a stick, had almost no bodily systems to regulate.
A handful of cells were enough to keep its body upright in the water or digest food in its primitive gut.
Newer animals, however, developed intricate internal systems.

Like a cardiovascular system with a heart that pumps blood, a respiratory system that takes in oxygen and eliminates carbon dioxide, an adaptable immune system that fights infections, and systems like these made body budgeting much more challenging.
It is less like a single bank account, and more like a whole accounting department in a sizable company.

These complex bodies needed something more than a handful of cells to ensure that water and blood and salt and oxygen and glucose and cortisol and sex hormones and dozens of other resources were regulated well to keep the body running efficiently.
They needed a command center.
You guessed it, a brain.
And so animals gradually evolved bigger bodies with more systems to maintain, and their handful of body budgeting cells evolved to become brains—brains of greater and greater complexity.
Fast forward a few hundred million years, and the earth is now littered with complicated brains of all kinds, including yours.

A brain that efficiently supervises over six hundred muscles in motion, balances dozens of different hormones, pumps blood at the rate of two thousand gallons per day, regulates the energy of billions of brain cells, digests food, excretes waste, and fights illness.
All of this non-stop for seventy-two years, give or take.
Your body budget is like thousands of financial accounts in a giant multinational corporation, and you have a brain that is up to this task.
And your body budgeting takes place in a massively complicated world, made even more challenging by all the other brains and bodies that you have to share it with.
So returning to our original question, why did a brain like yours evolve?
The answer is not actually answerable.
Why?
Because evolution does not act with purpose, and there is no why.
But we can say what is your brain's most important job?
It is not rationality, it is not emotion, it is not imagination or creativity or empathy.
Your brain's most important job is to control your body, to manage allostasis.
By predicting energy needs before they arise, you can efficiently make worthwhile movements and survive.

Your brain continually invests your energy in the hopes of earning a good return, such as food, shelter, affection, physical protection, so you can perform nature's most vital task: passing your genes on to the next generation.
In short, your brain's most important job is not thinking; it is running a little worm body that, well, has become very, very complicated.
Of course, your brain does think and feel and imagine and create hundreds of other experiences, such as letting you read and understand a book, like this book.
But all those mental capacities are a consequence of a central mission to keep you alive and well by managing your body budget.
Everything your brain creates, from memories to hallucinations, from ecstasy to shame, is part of this mission.

Sometimes your brain budgets for the short term, like when you drink a cup of coffee to stay up late and finish a project, knowing that you are borrowing energy that you will have to pay for tomorrow.

Other times your brain budgets for the long term, like when you spend years to learn a difficult skill, such as math or carpentry, that requires a sustained investment, but ultimately helps you to survive and prosper.
You and I do not experience our every thought, every feeling of happiness or anger or awe.
We do not experience every hug we give or receive, every kindness we extend, and every insult we bear as a deposit or a withdrawal in our metabolic budgets.
But under the hood, that is what is happening.
This idea is key to understanding how your brain works, and in turn how to stay healthy and live a longer and more meaningful life.
This little evolutionary story is the beginning of a longer tale about your brain and the other brains around you.

In the next seven short lessons, we will take a tour of the remarkable scientific findings in neuroscience, physiology, and anthropology that have revolutionized our understanding of what is really happening inside your skull.
You will learn what makes the human brain distinctive in the animal kingdom, which is full of astonishing brains.
And you will explore how infant brains gradually transform into adult brains.
You will discover how different kinds of human minds can arise from a single human brain structure.
We will even tackle the question of reality.
What gives us the power to invent customs, rules, and civilizations?
